did_you_know.text: Did you know? David fled from Naioth in Ramah and directly asked Jonathan, “What have I done, and what is my offense that Saul is seeking my life?” Thus, the chapter opens with a conflict between David’s claim and Jonathan’s trust in his father.
Did you know? David and Jonathan arranged to test Saul’s intentions during the New Moon feast. David planned to be absent from the feast and hide in the field until the third evening.
Did you know? David asked Jonathan to explain his absence by saying that he had gone to Bethlehem, his hometown, to take part in the family sacrifice—a meal held for the occasion.
Did you know? Jonathan swore to find out how Saul felt toward David and report the answer to him. He promised not to hide the information from David, whether Saul’s response was good or bad.

Did you know? Jonathan asked David to show kindness not only to him but also to his household and descendants in the future. In this way, their covenant took on lasting significance beyond the immediate danger.

Did you know? Jonathan planned to use the shooting of arrows as an agreed-upon signal: if he told the boy that the arrows were in front of him, it would be a message of safety; if he said they were farther away, David would have to flee.
Did you know? David hid in the field, while Saul sat in his usual place at the New Moon feast. David’s seat remained empty, but on the first day Saul still did not conclude that anything was wrong.

Did you know? After Jonathan explained that David had gone to Bethlehem, Saul became angry with him and accused him of siding with Jesse’s son. Saul claimed that as long as David lived, Jonathan’s kingdom would not be established.

Did you know? Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan, making Jonathan realize that his father’s decision to kill David was final. The act was also directed at Jonathan himself, who had tried to defend David.

Did you know? Jonathan shot the arrows beyond the boy and called out to him to hurry, thereby conveying to David that he had to escape. The boy himself did not know the meaning of the signal; only Jonathan and David understood it.
